what: Phasor Twin is a two-cylinder, externally driven kinematic model of the Stirling cycle's phase relation. One SPIKE medium motor drives a 40-tooth idler gear on its output shaft; the idler drives a 16-tooth gear on each of two vertical crank shafts, so both shafts turn 1:1 in the same direction at 2.5 times the motor speed. Each 40 LDU crank throw (16 mm) moves a 7L connecting rod whose small end is pinned to the vertical pin of an unfitted pneumatic cylinder rod. Those cylinders have no hoses, valve, pump or air: they are only linear guides, so each piston follows the pure crank-slider law. The two crank plates are clocked 90 degrees apart. The program turns the motor two full turns forward at 45 degrees per second, holds, returns to the saved pose, and holds again; both pistons, both rods and both crank plates are passive.
try: Load the model, press Reset, then Run. Watch the two horizontal piston rods at the same time.
Find the moments when one piston is at the end of its stroke. Where is the other piston then? With a 90-degree throw phase it should be near the middle of its stroke and moving fastest.
Plot the two piston displacements against each other while the crank turns. At a 90-degree phase the pair should trace a closed loop; the loop is the kinematic area that the Stirling cycle needs.

Load 'Phasor Twin — in phase (control)' instead: its second crank plate is clocked to the same angle. Both rods now move together, the loop collapses to a straight line, and the strokes stay the same.
why: In the isothermal Schmidt picture of an alpha Stirling engine the hot-space and cold-space volumes vary sinusoidally and must be about 90 degrees out of phase, otherwise the pressure-volume diagram encloses no area and the engine produces no net work. For two crank-slider pistons on one crank angle theta, the displacement is x(theta) = r sin(theta) + sqrt(L^2 - r^2 cos^2(theta)), and the rod-length term is an even function of theta, so all of its harmonics are even. When the two throws differ by phi, every even harmonic of one piston integrates to zero against the other piston's fundamental, leaving the cross loop of exactly pi r^2 sin(phi). That is why the two cases differ so sharply: at 90 degrees the pair encloses a circle-like loop, and at 0 degrees it encloses nothing. In the simulator the measured loop area is 805.8 mm² per crank turn, against 804.25 mm² predicted, and about 4 mm² in the in-phase control, with 32.00 mm strokes on both pistons.
matters: Stirling engines, free-piston machines and many pumps and compressors depend on a deliberate phase between two moving volumes; a wrong phase gives motion but no cycle area. The same quadrature idea appears in encoder signals, in vibration absorbers and in the two outputs of a differential, where a 90-degree relation separates a magnitude from a direction.
question: When the two crank throws are exactly 90 degrees apart, what closed shape do the two piston displacements trace against each other, and what is its area for a 16 mm throw?
answer: They trace a closed loop whose area is pi times r squared, about 804.25 mm^2 for r = 16 mm. With the throws in phase the same two pistons trace a straight line and the area is zero, while both strokes stay 32 mm. The engine cannot run on the in-phase case because its cycle area disappears.
further: Clock the second crank plate to 45 or 135 degrees and predict the loop area with pi r^2 sin(phi) before you measure it. Which clocking is easiest to set with the gear teeth?

Replace the 16-tooth crank gears with 24-tooth gears and a 24-tooth idler; the crank-to-motor ratio becomes 1:1. Does the phase law change? It should not, because the law depends on crank angle, not on motor angle.

The two pneumatic cylinders are only guides here. Fit hoses to a real valve and pump and the model becomes a pneumatic actuator, but then the piston motion is no longer the pure crank-slider law and the loop test no longer applies.
formula: x_i(θ) = x0 + r sin(θ + φ_i) + √(L² − r² cos²(θ + φ_i)); r = 16 mm, L = 48 mm. Loop area A = ∮ x_A dx_B = π r² sin φ: 804.25 mm² at φ = 90°, 0 at φ = 0°. Simulator: 805.8 mm² per crank turn at 90°, about 4 mm² in phase.
